parts.title: Booking a walking tour
parts.context: A man books a guided walk for a group for his mother's birthday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a company to book a guided walking tour for a group. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: Heritage Walks, Eleni speaking.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Hello. I'd like to book a guided walk for a group, please. It's for my mother's birthday, and she loves history.

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: How lovely. I'll take some details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The walk is for a birthday, so 'birthday' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Ben Wallace. That's W-A-L-L-A-C-E.

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: Thank you, Mr Wallace. How many people will there be?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: I thought ten, but a couple more have decided to come, so twelve.

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: And which date would you like?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Saturday the seventeenth of May.

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: That's fine. Where would the group like to meet?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Outside the cathedral, if that's all right. It's easy for everyone to find.

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: Are there any special needs we should know about?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Most of the group are over sixty, so we'd like a gentle pace, with places to sit.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: We have three tours. The Old Town walk lasts two hours, and it costs twelve pounds per person. It's the most popular, and it's quite gentle.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: That sounds perfect. And the others?

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: The Ghost walk is ninety minutes, in the evening, and it costs fourteen pounds. It's not really suitable for people who want a quiet pace, because there are lots of steps.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: No, I think not. What's the third?

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: The Castle and Gardens tour. It lasts three hours, and it costs twenty pounds, which includes a cream tea at the castle café. It's a coach tour, so there's not much walking.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: That sounds lovely for my mother. Do you give discounts for groups?

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: Yes, there's a fifteen percent discount for groups of more than ten, which applies to you.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Excellent. I'll take the Old Town walk. Can I pay by card?

script.speaker: eleni
script.text: Yes, and I'll email you a receipt and the meeting point.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A tour of an old town
parts.context: A guide introduces a walking tour.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide introducing a walking tour of an old town. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: costa
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to our walk round the Old Town. I'm Maria Costa, and I've been a guide here for ten years. Please look at the map. We're at the Old Bridge, at the bottom, and the main street goes straight ahead, to the junction in the middle of the town.

script.speaker: costa
script.text: On the way up, on the left, is the museum, in an old merchant's house. We'll visit it at the end of the tour. On the right, in a big building with a green roof, is the Town Hall.

script.speaker: costa
script.text: At the junction, we turn right, and above the junction on the right of the main street is the Clock Tower, which you'll see from all over the town.

script.speaker: costa
script.text: On the left, in the top corner, is the cathedral, and in the top right corner, behind the Clock Tower, is the Market Square, where the market is held every Saturday morning. The library, above the junction on the left, and the old prison on the lower left aren't on our route.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: costa
script.text: A few notes on what we'll see. The cathedral isn't famous for its tower, although that is tall, but for its stained glass windows, which date from the twelfth century and are among the oldest in the country.

script.speaker: costa
script.text: The Clock Tower was built in the seventeen hundreds, to replace an older one that burned down. People often assume it's medieval, but it isn't.

script.speaker: costa
script.text: At noon every day, little wooden figures come out of the clock and strike the bell. It's very popular, so we'll arrange to be in the square at five to twelve.

script.speaker: costa
script.text: The tour takes about two hours, and there are places to sit along the way. If anyone gets tired, just tell me.

script.speaker: costa
script.text: And we'll finish at a small café, near the museum, where you can have a hot drink, and I'll answer any more questions. Shall we start?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A model of a library design
parts.context: Two architecture students plan a model.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two architecture students, Freda and Kai, planning a model of a library design. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: Kai, we need to decide how to build the model of our library design. What scale did the tutor say?

script.speaker: kai
script.text: One to a hundred, so that the whole building fits on one table. A scale of one to fifty would be too big.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: Right. And it's a public library, not a university one, isn't it? That affects the design, with so many different users.

script.speaker: kai
script.text: Yes, for the whole community, from children to older people. That's why we included a children's area on the ground floor.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: Which feature are we most proud of?

script.speaker: kai
script.text: The reading garden on the roof. It's unusual, and it's the first thing the examiners will notice.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: What will be the main difficulty in building the model?

script.speaker: kai
script.text: The curved roof. Cutting curves is hard, and the card tends to wrinkle.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: How shall we divide the work?

script.speaker: kai
script.text: I'll build the structure, since I'm better with a knife, and you can do the landscaping and the lettering.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: Let's choose the materials. The walls first.

script.speaker: kai
script.text: Foam board, because it's light, easy to cut, and it keeps its shape.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: The roof?

script.speaker: kai
script.text: Thin card, so that we can bend it into a curve. Paper would be too weak.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: The windows?

script.speaker: kai
script.text: Clear plastic, from a sheet. We can stick it behind the openings, and it will look like real glass.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: And the floors? We want to be able to lift them out to show the inside.

script.speaker: kai
script.text: Balsa wood. It's thin and strong, and doesn't bend under the weight of the furniture.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: And the trees in the garden?

script.speaker: kai
script.text: Small pieces of sponge, painted green. It's the classic way, and it looks good enough.

script.speaker: freda
script.text: I'll buy the materials on Saturday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: garden cities
parts.context: A lecture on the garden city movement.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about garden cities. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today we'll look at an idea which has influenced town planning for over a century: the garden city.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: At the end of the nineteenth century, the cities of Britain were crowded and dirty, while the countryside was losing its people. An English reformer named Ebenezer Howard had an idea. In a book published in eighteen ninety-eight, he proposed that a new kind of town could combine the best of the town and the country.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Each garden city would be limited in size, with about thirty thousand people. When it reached that number, a new town would be built nearby, instead of the existing one growing without limit.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: A garden city would be surrounded by a belt of farmland, which would keep the countryside close to everyone and prevent the town from spreading. The land would be owned by the community, so that any increase in its value would benefit the residents, and not private landowners.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The layout was carefully planned. Houses had gardens, and the streets were wide and lined with trees. Shops were grouped in the town centre, and factories were kept in a separate area on the edge, so that workers could live near their jobs without the smoke and noise.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The first garden city was begun in nineteen oh three, and a second followed in the nineteen twenties. They were successful, although they did not become the cheap communities that Howard had imagined.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The ideas had a lasting influence. After the Second World War, the British government built a series of new towns, which borrowed much from the garden city plan, including the green spaces, and the separation of homes from industry.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The idea has also been criticised. Many garden suburbs were designed for people who owned cars, and critics argue that they make people depend on cars to get around. Even so, Howard's vision continues to inspire planners who want more green space in cities. Next week we'll look at skyscrapers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
